Excess capacity is the gap between the output at minimum ATC and the output the firm chooses: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">60 - 40 = 20</annotation></semantics></math> sandwiches per hour.
Allocative efficiency needs P = MC. Maple Row's price ($8) is above its marginal cost ($5), so buyers value one more sandwich more than it costs to make, and too few are made.
options: P = ATC means zero economic profit; efficiency needs P = MC.
Zero profit says nothing about whether P = MC.
$8 is above $6.50; the gap from minimum ATC is about productive efficiency.

why.correct: Productive efficiency means producing at minimum ATC. Maple Row produces 40 sandwiches at an ATC of $8, not 60 at $6.50, so it is not productively efficient: that gap is its excess capacity.
options: Right: ATC of $8 is above the minimum of $6.50.
Zero profit at a point on the falling part of ATC is not minimum cost.
MR = MC maximizes profit; it does not put the firm at minimum ATC.
Its price equals ATC at 40 sandwiches.

why.correct: Fennel and Fire's economic profit signaled that this kind of truck earned more than the owners' next best use of their money and time, and entry was easy.
options: Entry follows economic profit; a demand change matters only through profit.
Right: profit attracts entry when there are no barriers.
Nothing in the description says so; entry was easy for any truck.

why.correct: With close substitutes nearby, some of its buyers switched, so its demand decreased (shifted left) and became more elastic, since buyers now had more choices.
options: More rivals take buyers away and add substitutes.
Buyers moved to the new trucks at every price, so demand itself shifted.
Right: fewer buyers at each price, and more substitutes.
More substitutes make demand more elastic, not less.

why.correct: Entry continues until each truck's demand is tangent to its ATC: price equals ATC and economic profit is zero (a normal profit).
options: Easy entry keeps going until economic profit is zero.
If losses appeared, trucks would leave until profit returned to zero.
Zero economic profit still covers the owner's opportunity costs; and P stays above MC.
Right: entry stops when the profit is gone.

why.correct: Successful differentiation makes buyers see fewer close substitutes, so demand rises (shifts right) and becomes less elastic, letting the truck raise its price, at least until rivals copy it.
options: Right: more loyal buyers with fewer substitutes in their eyes.
Advertising that works draws buyers in, not away.
Differentiation moves away from a horizontal demand curve.
Advertising costs money, so it raises ATC; its aim is to raise demand.

why.correct: Price and cost on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal. D slopes down and just touches ATC; MR is below D; MC crosses ATC at its minimum.
Find the quantity where MR = MC and go up to demand. In the long run that point is where demand is tangent to ATC, so P = ATC and economic profit is zero.
Entry takes customers away, so this firm's demand shifts left (MR moves with it). Costs do not change. Demand keeps shifting until it is tangent to ATC.
At the quantity where MR = MC, ATC is above the price read from demand. The loss is the rectangle between ATC and the price, from zero to that quantity.
When rivals exit, their customers move to the remaining firms, so this firm's demand shifts right until it is tangent to ATC and the loss is gone.

Both end with zero economic profit. But the monopolistically competitive firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve, so it produces short of minimum ATC (excess capacity) and charges a price above MC.
options: Right: excess capacity.
Right: P > MC, so the outcome is not allocatively efficient.
Easy entry drives economic profit to zero in both structures.
Price equals ATC (the tangency) in the long run.

why.correct: Profit draws entry; entry takes buyers from each firm, shifting its demand left; that continues until demand is tangent to ATC; then profit is zero and entry stops.
Its demand curve slopes down, so the tangency with ATC is on the falling part of ATC, to the left of the minimum.
Both face a downward-sloping demand curve, so both have MR below demand and charge a price above MC. They differ in entry: easy in monopolistic competition, blocked in monopoly.

Entry drives a monopolistic competitor's profit to zero.
Monopolistic competitors sell close, though not identical, substitutes.

why.correct: Ember: if Tidewater prices high, $80 from Low beats $60 from High; if Tidewater prices low, $40 from Low beats $20 from High. Low wins both comparisons, so Low is dominant. Tidewater's payoffs are the mirror image, so Low is dominant for it too. Neither gains by switching alone from (Low, Low), the only Nash equilibrium.
A dominant strategy is better whatever the rival does, so it takes one comparison for each of Tidewater's choices: 80 > 60 when Tidewater prices high and 40 > 20 when Tidewater prices low.
options: Right: Low is better against each of Tidewater's choices.
The single largest payoff does not prove a strategy wins against each choice of the rival.
That compares combined payoffs, which says nothing about Ember's best choice.

why.correct: Add the two payoffs in each cell: 120, 100, 100 and 80. Both pricing high gives $120 together.
From (High, High), each cafe gains by switching alone to Low ($80 instead of $60), so High is not stable. Each one's dominant strategy is Low, and the result is worse for both: a prisoner's dilemma.

Producing more is dominant for Kiln Rock (70 > 50 if Gray Ridge keeps the quota, 40 > 30 if it produces more) and, by the same numbers, for Gray Ridge. So both produce more and earn 40 each, and neither gains by switching alone.

Gray Ridge would switch: 40 from producing more beats 30.

Both producing more is stable: neither firm gains by switching alone.

why.correct: Collusion pays the group, but each firm gains by cheating whatever the other does, and the agreement cannot be enforced in court. So each has an incentive to produce more.
options: Keeping the quota gives each firm 50, the outcome with the most joint profit.

Producing more raises a firm's own profit against either choice.

why.correct: Orrin: if Velo picks Friday, Tuesday is better (40 > 20); if Velo picks Tuesday, Friday is better (50 > 10). Its best choice changes, so it has no dominant strategy, and Velo's payoffs mirror Orrin's. No dominant strategy needs both comparisons, showing the best choice changes: Tuesday is better if Velo picks Friday (40 > 20), and Friday is better if Velo picks Tuesday (50 > 10).
